persona.role: experienced landscape architect and project manager

sent_to_model:
I'd like some help with a reply on a gardening forum. Someone is considering a portable greenhouse on their deck in the PNW, and after 30 years as a Landscape Architect/Project Manager I have quite a few thoughts! I want to suggest a permanent glass garden room and show them what they could gain by thinking beyond a seasonal greenhouse. I'd like to give them enough practical detail about materials, planting, heating and construction to picture the possibilities. I'm pretty firm about what our wet climate does to wood. I also want to make the case for getting a good landscape company involved and doing the project in affordable stages. I don't know their deck height or how it meets the house, so those are questions. And I ought to allow for them being renters, which would change the whole discussion.

- Proposed temporary greenhouse measures 8'x20'; annual assembly and dismantling would be considerable work.
- Low decks or decks below the main floor are the condition for the proposed paved floor, garden walls and planters.
- Professional background: 30 years as Landscape Architect/Project Manager in the Pacific Northwest.
- Need deck height above ground, whether level with main floor, and whether access involves stepping down.
- Room could support vegetables and exotic plants throughout the year, with attractive containers, raised planting areas and comfortable furniture.
- Suggested floor: dove gray Roman Cobble Pavers, 7X9X2 inches, laid without mortar; pressure-treated dimensional lumber forms perimeter.
- Passive solar needs sun-facing glazing, insulation to retain warmth, and ventilation for overheating.
- Landscape design-build firms can quote the complete job, including low voltage lighting, especially useful in the PNW.
- Wall height from paving through cap: 18 inches. Concrete cap approximately two feet wide and two inches thick.
- French doors or large folding doors connect house and garden room; opening doors could transfer solar warmth indoors and reduce heating bills.
- Composite decking used for clients: greater purchase cost and predrilled screw holes.
- Gray natural stone is expensive and difficult for inexperienced builders; CMUs offer an alternative and increasingly natural appearance.
- Include integrated planters and sitting walls; sufficiently large raised beds could hold trees or vegetables.
- Recommend 6X6 structural posts, substantial glazing, concrete and paving; visible 4X4 posts look undersized beside a house.
- Wood stove or open fireplace for comfort and atmosphere; also a room-sized cadet heater.
- Writer associates composite decking with no maintenance and lower home insurance costs; wet wooden decking can become dangerously slippery.
- Dove gray recommended across paving, concrete, CMU walls, timber garden structures and edging; gravel also particularly suitable locally.
- Permanent glazed room could serve for entertaining or private relaxation; writer expects improved property value and easier resale.
- Usually persuaded clients against attached wooden decks; clients determined to have decking were offered composite lumber.
- Used an ashlar arrangement combining three or four block sizes; more demanding to assemble but worthwhile.
- Other deck colors tend to appear dirty or moldy. Garden colors should harmonize with surrounding woodland.
- Wooden decks perform poorly in the PNW; believes they can become liabilities and decrease property value.
- A home improvement of this scale deserves experienced construction. Learning masonry on this project would be a poor investment decision.
- Encourage a larger permanent project, divided into affordable phases; competitive landscape firms can offer strong value and coordinate the necessary trades.
- Can suggest landscape companies depending on location, subject to forum rules; alternatively explain selection criteria. Could provide example photographs if wanted.
- Leave open the possibility of renting: portability would make much more sense if the property isn't theirs.

(About me: experienced landscape architect and project manager, Pacific Northwest, United States. Length: it should come to roughly 800-2,000 words.)

must_cover: Propose a permanent glazed garden room and explain its advantages over a seasonal greenhouse.
Describe suitable materials, planting possibilities and heating considerations for the wet Pacific Northwest climate.
Recommend professional landscape construction and dividing the project into affordable stages.
Ask the deck height and whether it is level with the house or requires stepping down; acknowledge renting could explain portability.
Explain why the writer discourages wooden decks in the wet Pacific Northwest climate.
